guideTitle: Best Propane Space Heaters for RV (2026)
metaTitle: Best Propane Space Heaters for RV
metaDescription: Six propane heaters compared on BTU output, runtime, oxygen sensors and ventilation needs for RVs, vans and campers, with CO alarm and moisture advice.
expertTake: The Mr. Heater Portable Buddy is the pick for most RV owners, with a 4,000 BTU low setting that suits a small camper and a 1 pound cylinder that needs no electricity. The Big Buddy suits larger rigs with its 20 pound tank hookup, and the Little Buddy suits a van. These are supplemental heaters, not replacements for the RV furnace. Skip vent-free heaters entirely if anyone in the rig has respiratory trouble or if your campground bans them.
introParagraphs: A propane space heater for an RV is a supplemental source that warms a small space without using battery power, which is why campers like them for cold mornings and power outages. The buying problem is that RV interiors are small, and most heaters are sized for larger rooms, so the box number is usually too much heat and too much moisture.

This guide explains how to size a heater to an RV's volume, what oxygen depletion sensors do and do not protect against, and how fuel consumption and ventilation change the decision. Start with the picks above for the shortlist, then read the reviews below to match a heater to your rig, your tank setup and the rules of your campground and jurisdiction.

products.name: Mr. Heater Portable Buddy 9,000 BTU Radiant Heater

specList.label: Runtime
specList.value: 5.4 h low, 2.4 h high on a 1 lb cylinder

products.description:
The Portable Buddy is the sensible heater for a small RV because its output matches the volume of the space. A camper interior of 100 to 250 square feet needs only a few thousand BTU to stay warm in mild cold, and the Buddy's 4,000 BTU low setting is closer to that than the 18,000 BTU units here. On high it puts out 9,000 BTU, enough to take the chill off a cold morning. It runs on a single 1 pound propane cylinder, and the maker quotes 5.4 hours on low and 2.4 hours on high.

The trade is cylinder consumption. Two and a half hours on high from a 1 pound cylinder is expensive heat, and you will want the optional Buddy hose and a 20 pound tank for overnight use. Compared with the Big Buddy it has half the high output and no fan, but it is lighter and cheaper. Compared with the Little Buddy at 3,800 BTU, it gives more than twice the high output for a modest size increase.

The safety design uses a pilot oxygen sensor that shuts the heater off if oxygen drops and a tip-over switch. These do not detect carbon monoxide, so a battery CO alarm in the RV is not optional. Vent-free heaters also add moisture, so crack a window. The maker lists indoor use, but check the manual and local rules for restrictions on recreational vehicles. Use only authorized accessories.
products.bestFor: RV owners who want a small, cylinder-fed backup heater for a camper under about 225 square feet.
pros: Low setting of 4,000 BTU suits a small camper interior
Oxygen depletion sensor and tip-over switch are built in
Runs on a 1 pound cylinder with no electricity
Maker rates it for indoor and outdoor use
cons: High setting uses a 1 lb cylinder in about 2.4 hours
No CO sensor, so a separate CO alarm is required
Adds moisture indoors, which causes window condensation

products.name: Mr. Heater Big Buddy Midnight Series 18,000 BTU

specList.label: Fuel
specList.value: Two 1 lb cylinders or 20 lb tank with hose

specList.label: Runtime
specList.value: Up to 96 h on low with a 20 lb tank

specList.label: Safety
specList.value: Self-extinguishing, low oxygen and tip-over shutoff

specList.label: Restriction
specList.value: Indoor use not approved in Canada or Massachusetts

products.description:
The Big Buddy is the upgrade when a camper is large, or when the weather is truly cold. It offers three settings at 4,000, 9,000 and 18,000 BTU and, per Mr. Heater, heats up to about 450 square feet. A built-in fan circulates the warm air, and electronic ignition starts it with a push of a button. With a 20 pound tank and the optional hose, the maker quotes up to 96 hours on low, which makes overnight use easy without swapping cylinders.

The trade is oversizing. At 18,000 BTU it is far more heat than most RV interiors can use, and the fan needs a power source, which adds a small draw. For a 25 foot travel trailer, the low and medium settings are what you will use, so the Big Buddy's value is the fuel economy at those settings with a big tank. Compared with the Portable Buddy, it doubles the high output and adds the fan. Compared with the ProCom 10,000 BTU, it is portable instead of wall-mounted.

The maker states indoor use is not approved in Canada or Massachusetts, so verify your jurisdiction. The Life Safety System includes self-extinguishing protection, a low oxygen shutoff and a tip-over shutdown. It does not detect carbon monoxide, so run a CO alarm. Moisture is a factor, so provide ventilation, and use only the authorized hose and filter.
products.bestFor: Owners of larger RVs and toy haulers, or anyone camping in cold weather who wants overnight fuel capacity.
pros: Three heat settings from 4,000 to 18,000 BTU
Maker quotes up to 96 hours on low with a 20 lb tank
Built-in fan moves warm air through the space
Electronic ignition lights with a push of a button
cons: Eighteen thousand BTU is far more than a small RV needs
Indoor use is not approved in Canada or Massachusetts
Hose and fuel filter are sold separately for a 20 lb tank

products.name: Mr. Heater Little Buddy 3,800 BTU Radiant Heater
products.description:
The Little Buddy is the pick for a van, a camper cab or a sleeping nook rather than a whole camper. It outputs a single setting of 3,800 BTU and heats up to about 95 square feet according to the maker, so it takes the edge off a small bunk space without cooking you. Its 8 inch round stand uses very little floor, and the unit connects directly to a 1 pound propane cylinder.

The limits are plain. With one output and no thermostat, it cannot back off, so you cycle it by hand. Compared with the Portable Buddy, it matches the Buddy's low setting of 4,000 BTU but gives no extra capacity for a cold morning. A 1 pound cylinder holds about 21,600 BTU, so at 3,800 BTU the heater runs roughly five and a half hours, which suits a few hours before bed but not an overnight run without a hose.

It has a tip-over switch and an automatic low oxygen shutoff, and a one-button ignition. It does not have a CO sensor, so a CO alarm is a must. Like all vent-free heaters, it makes moisture, and burning a pound of propane produces about 1.6 pounds of water. Crack a window, and do not sleep with it running in a closed space.
products.bestFor: Van dwellers and small camper owners who need a minimal heater for a bunk or a cab.
pros: Quiet single setting suits a small sleeping area
Eight inch base takes very little floor space
Automatic low oxygen shutoff and tip-over switch
Connects directly to a 1 lb cylinder with no hose
cons: Single output with no way to turn the heat down
A 1 lb cylinder lasts about 5.5 hours at 3,800 BTU
Heats only about 95 square feet by the maker's figure

products.name: ProCom 10,000 BTU Ventless Blue Flame Heater
products.description:
The ProCom blue flame heater is a fixed, thermostat-controlled alternative to the Buddy line. It produces up to 10,000 BTU, uses a thermostat with high, medium and low settings, and mounts on a wall with the included hardware or stands on base feet. It needs no electricity, which is appealing in an RV when the battery is low. The maker lists a 500 square foot heating area, a number that is optimistic for a camper with poor insulation.

The design is a vent-free blue flame heater. That means combustion products, including moisture and trace carbon monoxide, are released into the room, so these units are designed with a pilot oxygen depletion sensor. The listing's claim that the sensor shuts the heater off if carbon monoxide is detected overstates what an ODS does. It senses low oxygen, and a CO alarm is still needed. Compared with the Portable Buddy, it has a thermostat but needs a connection to a propane supply, so it is a more permanent installation.

Vent-free wall heaters are often not permitted in RVs and manufactured homes, so check the label and the manual before you install one. It makes sense in a garage, a shop or a cabin. If you plan to use it in a camper, confirm it is rated for that use and run a CO alarm and fresh air.
products.bestFor: Cabin, garage or toy hauler owners who want a thermostat-controlled, wall-mounted heater.
pros: Thermostat holds temperature without constant adjustment
Wall mount or feet gives flexible placement
Needs no electricity to run
ANSI certified with a pilot oxygen sensor
cons: Vent-free wall heaters may not be permitted in RVs
Maker's 500 sq ft figure is optimistic for a camper
Releases moisture and combustion products indoors

products.name: WELLUCK 18,000 BTU Portable Cabinet Propane Heater

specList.label: Runtime
specList.value: Up to 69 h on low with 20 lb tank

specList.label: Fuel
specList.value: 20 lb tank with QCC hose and regulator

products.description:
The WELLUCK is a cabinet-style heater on wheels, designed for garages, patios and job sites, and it earns a place here as the choice for a large toy hauler or a camper with a garage space. It offers three output settings at 6,000, 12,000 and 18,000 BTU and, with a 20 pound tank and its QCC hose with a built-in regulator, the maker quotes up to 69 hours on the lowest setting.

The minimum setting is the problem for a small RV. Its low of 6,000 BTU is half again higher than the Portable Buddy's 4,000 BTU low, so it will overheat a small camper quickly. Compared with the Big Buddy, it has a lower minimum than 9,000 but no fan, and with wheels it moves around a space. Compared with the Little Buddy, it is a bigger and heavier machine and not meant for a van.

It folds flat to about 15 centimeters for storage and has four swivel casters, two with brakes. A dedicated ignition setting purges air before lighting to prevent a flare-up. It has an oxygen depletion sensor and tip-over protection, but, as with every heater here, it has no CO sensor and the listing says to use it only in well-ventilated spaces. This is a lesser-known brand, so check warranty terms.
products.bestFor: Toy hauler and workshop users who need a mobile, wheeled heater with a big runtime on a 20 lb tank.
pros: Dedicated ignition setting purges air before lighting
Folds to about 15 cm thin and rolls on casters
Up to 69 hours on low with a 20 lb tank
QCC hose with built-in regulator is included per listing
cons: Lowest setting of 6,000 BTU is too hot for a small camper
Lesser-known brand with limited service history
No fan to move warm air around the space

products.name: ProCom 20,000 BTU Ventless Blue Flame Heater
products.description:
This larger ProCom is included to show where the size line sits, not as a camper heater. At 20,000 BTU the maker says it heats up to 950 square feet. That is more than most RV interiors can use by a wide margin: a 30 foot travel trailer is roughly 200 square feet. The unit has the same thermostat, wall-mount or feet layout and pilot oxygen sensor as the 10,000 BTU model.

Its place is a fifth wheel garage, a large toy hauler or a workshop attached to a camper lot. Compared with the Big Buddy's 18,000 BTU top setting, it offers a thermostat and wall mounting but no portability. Compared with the ProCom 10,000 BTU, it doubles output, but a thermostat that cycles a 20,000 BTU burner will make a small space swing between hot and cold.

It is vent-free, so combustion moisture and exhaust enter the space. The same cautions apply: it is not a substitute for the RV's own vented furnace, vent-free wall heaters may not be permitted in recreational vehicles, and a CO alarm and ventilation are essential. Check the label and the manual, and consider a smaller heater for a camper.
products.bestFor: Large toy haulers, garages and workshops where 20,000 BTU is justified.
pros: Thermostat control with three heat settings
Heats a large space per the maker's 950 sq ft figure
Wall-mount hardware and base feet included
Pilot oxygen sensor and ANSI certification
cons: Twenty thousand BTU is oversized for nearly all campers
Vent-free design may not be allowed in an RV
Fixed placement, so it cannot move with you

buyingCriteria.explanation: A small RV interior is roughly 100 to 250 square feet, and in mild cold needs only a few thousand BTU. The Mr. Heater Little Buddy at 3,800 BTU is rated for about 95 square feet, the Portable Buddy for 225 square feet and the Big Buddy for up to 450 square feet. Oversizing makes the heater cycle on high, overheating the space and wasting fuel. Choose a heater with a low setting near 4,000 BTU, and a lower BTU is better for tight rigs.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Oxygen depletion sensor and what it does not do
buyingCriteria.explanation: An oxygen depletion sensor shuts the heater off if oxygen in the room falls below a threshold. It does not detect carbon monoxide, despite what some listings say, as in the ProCom listing. Every heater here also needs a battery-powered CO alarm in the RV, because incomplete combustion can create CO before oxygen drops. The Buddy heaters and the WELLUCK include an oxygen sensor and a tip-over switch.

Burning propane produces water, about 1.6 pounds of water for every pound of propane. An 18,000 BTU heater burning for an hour makes roughly 1.4 pounds of water, which condenses on cold windows and walls and can lead to mold. Crack a vent or window to move the humid air out, or run a small dehumidifier. Vent-free heaters are a bigger moisture problem in a small, tight RV than in a house.

A 1 pound cylinder holds about 21,600 BTU. The Portable Buddy on high at 9,000 BTU lasts about 2.4 hours, and on low about 5.4 hours. A 20 pound tank with a hose stretches that: Mr. Heater quotes up to 96 hours on low for the Big Buddy and WELLUCK quotes 69 hours. For overnight use, plan on a 20 pound tank and the right hose, not a stack of 1 pound cylinders.

Vent-free heaters carry labels that restrict where they can be used. The Big Buddy listing says indoor use is not approved in Canada or Massachusetts, and vent-free wall heaters are often not allowed in recreational vehicles. Many campgrounds, RV makers and insurers have their own rules. Read the label and the manual, and check local rules, before using any of these in a camper.

Electronic or push-button ignition, a tip-over shutoff and a stable base reduce the chances of an accident in a small, moving space. The Mr. Heater models and the WELLUCK include tip-over protection, and the WELLUCK adds a dedicated ignition setting that purges air before lighting. A wide stable base matters in a camper where the floor shifts under you. Use only the authorized hoses and filters.

specDecoder.meaning: A measure of heat output. One BTU is the heat to raise a pound of water one degree Fahrenheit.
specDecoder.watchFor: Heated-area figures such as 500 or 950 square feet assume a well-insulated, tall space, not an RV.

specDecoder.meaning: An oxygen depletion sensor shuts off the gas if oxygen levels fall too low.
specDecoder.watchFor: It is not a carbon monoxide sensor. The ProCom listing claims otherwise.

specDecoder.meaning: A radiant heater glows a ceramic or metal face to warm objects and people directly. A blue flame heater warms the air convectively.
specDecoder.watchFor: Radiant heat feels stronger on you than the BTU suggests, and blue flame is better at heating the whole room.

specDecoder.meaning: The time a 1 pound propane cylinder lasts, which depends on the setting.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Portable Buddy's 2.4 hours on high is short. Plan for a 20 pound tank.

specDecoder.meaning: A heater that releases its combustion products into the room rather than outdoors.
specDecoder.watchFor: It adds moisture and relies on room air. Provide fresh air and a CO alarm.

howWeEvaluated.title: Output matched to RV volume
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared BTU settings against a typical RV interior of 100 to 250 square feet. The Little Buddy at 3,800 BTU, the Portable Buddy at 4,000 and 9,000, and the Big Buddy at 4,000 to 18,000 were treated as best fit. Units whose low setting was 6,000 BTU or more were penalized.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety features
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for an oxygen depletion sensor, tip-over shutoff, ignition design and self-extinguishing materials. We also noted where a listing overstated what a sensor does.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fuel and runtime
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared quoted runtimes, such as 5.4 hours on low from a 1 pound cylinder for the Portable Buddy and 96 hours on a 20 pound tank for the Big Buddy. A heater that cannot easily connect to a larger tank was rated lower for overnight use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Use-rating and restrictions
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted maker restrictions, including the Big Buddy's Canada and Massachusetts limitation, and the common prohibition of vent-free wall heaters in RVs. Items without clear ratings were flagged.

howWeEvaluated.title: Portability and placement
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared weight, stands, wall mounts and wheels. The Buddy heaters sit on the floor, the ProCom heaters wall mount, and the WELLUCK rolls.

howToChoose.subheading: Portable Radiant vs Fixed Blue Flame
howToChoose.intro: Two ways to heat a space with propane.

cards.label: Portable radiant
cards.text: The Mr. Heater Little Buddy, Portable Buddy and Big Buddy warm people and objects directly and sit on the floor. They are easy to store and use a 1 pound cylinder or a hose to a 20 pound tank.

cards.label: Fixed blue flame
cards.text: The ProCom 10,000 and 20,000 BTU units heat the air, hold a thermostat setting and mount on a wall. They are better for a garage or cabin and often not permitted in RVs.

howToChoose.note: Choose portable radiant for a camper or van. Choose fixed blue flame for a cabin, garage or workshop.

howToChoose.intro: How you will supply the propane.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A battery CO alarm in the sleeping area, a heater with an oxygen sensor and tip-over shutoff, and fresh air. Do not run a vent-free heater while sleeping in a sealed space.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Mr. Heater Portable Buddy and Big Buddy have both the oxygen sensor and tip-over shutoff. Use the lowest setting and crack a window. The RV's built-in vented furnace is the safer way to heat overnight.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You camp in cold weather or need overnight heat. The Mr. Heater Big Buddy gives low-setting economy with a 20 lb tank and a fan.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You only need a bit of warmth for a few hours. The Little Buddy and Portable Buddy cover that with a 1 lb cylinder.

maintenance.task: Inspect hoses and fittings for leaks
maintenance.interval: Before each season and each connection
maintenance.why: A brushed soapy water solution on fittings shows bubbles from a leak. Propane leaks are a fire and asphyxiation hazard in a small space.

maintenance.interval: Per the maker, often every 5 to 10 years
maintenance.why: Rubber hoses crack with age. Use only authorized accessories, as the makers warn.

maintenance.task: Clean dust from the burner and pilot
maintenance.why: Dust and spider webs block the pilot and cause poor combustion. A soft brush and low-pressure air help.
A battery alarm is the only device that detects CO in the RV. Replace the battery yearly and the unit per its date.
Follow the manual's test steps. A stuck switch could fail to shut off on a fall.
Cylinders must stay upright, strapped and away from heat. Do not store them inside the cabin.

faq.q: Is it safe to use a propane heater inside an RV?
faq.a: It is a judgment call with real risks. Mr. Heater rates the Buddy line for indoor use, but vent-free heaters produce moisture and can produce carbon monoxide, and some jurisdictions and campgrounds restrict them. If you use one, run a battery CO alarm, crack a window, use the lowest setting and never leave it running while you sleep. The RV's vented furnace is the safer main heat source.

faq.q: Does the oxygen depletion sensor protect against carbon monoxide?
faq.a: No. An ODS shuts the heater off when oxygen falls below a threshold. Carbon monoxide can form from incomplete combustion before oxygen is low, which is why a CO alarm is required. Some listings blur this, but the sensor and the alarm are different safety devices.

faq.q: How much propane will a heater use?
faq.a: A 1 pound cylinder holds about 21,600 BTU. At 9,000 BTU an hour that lasts about 2.4 hours, and at 4,000 BTU about 5.4 hours. A 20 pound tank holds about 430,000 BTU, so on low it lasts days. Burn rate rises with the setting, so use the lowest that keeps the RV comfortable.

faq.q: Why are my RV windows wet when the heater runs?
faq.a: Burning propane produces about 1.6 pounds of water for every pound burned, and a vent-free heater releases it into the room. The water condenses on cold surfaces. Crack a window or roof vent, and consider a small dehumidifier. Persistent condensation can cause mold.

faq.q: What size heater do I need for a 25 foot travel trailer?
faq.a: A 25 foot trailer is roughly 150 to 200 square feet. In mild cold, 4,000 to 9,000 BTU is plenty. The Portable Buddy's low and high settings cover it, while an 18,000 BTU unit is oversized and will cycle between too hot and too cold.

faq.q: Can I run a propane heater at high altitude?
faq.a: Altitude reduces the oxygen available for combustion, and oxygen depletion sensors may trip more often above about 7,000 feet. Makers often publish altitude limits and some require a different orifice. Check the manual for your heater.
